Dear Secretary Reese: 
The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), through this filing,1 
submits proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve 
Markets Tariff (“Tariff”),2 to establish certain Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large 
Loads (the “IRR Proposal”).3  The IRR Proposal is responsive to several of the concerns raised by 
the Commission in the Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act4 
in Docket No. EL26-70-000 by proposing visibility, ramp rate, and disturbance ride-through 
requirements applicable to Large Loads, along with transition provisions to minimize disruption 
to commercial arrangements.  Other issues raised in the Show Cause Order, including the 
development of additional transmission products for Large Loads and associated study processes, 
cost shifting, protections against cost shifts and the treatment of generation service to electrically 
proximate to Large Loads, will be addressed through MISO’s forthcoming Large Load proposals.

MISO requests that the Tariff revisions submitted herewith be made effective December 4, 
2026, which is not less than sixty (60) days nor more than one-hundred and twenty (120) days 
from the date of this filing.  As discussed below and in the supporting testimony of Ms. BeiBei Li, 
action is needed in the near term to enhance the available tools to address the reliability impacts 
associated with the impending interconnection of Load, including the anticipated interconnection 
of significant Large Loads. 
I. 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
The MISO region is experiencing a significant increase in both the scale and pace of Large 
Load development.  MISO’s 2026 Long-Term Load Forecast5 indicates that the region is 
experiencing load growth at levels not seen in decades, driven in large part by unprecedented large 
load activity and accelerating project announcements.  Data centers and advanced manufacturing 
are among the primary drivers of this growth, with some projects seeking to develop on timelines 
significantly shorter than those traditionally associated with generation and transmission 
infrastructure.  This combination of increased volume and accelerated development is changing 
the manner in which MISO must plan for and reliably integrate new load.   
 
As this growth has emerged, MISO, its member states, and stakeholders have been 
developing multiple initiatives to address evolving system conditions and to support timely, cost-
effective and reliable interconnection of Large Loads.  For example, MISO’s Expedited Project 
Review (EPR) Process and Expedited Resource Addition Studies (ERAS) complement MISO’s 
determination of needed additional transmission infrastructure, which are being planned and 
implemented through the Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue (JTIQ) and Long Range 
Transmission Plan (LRTP) processes.  An additional and critical proposal, the Zero Injection 
Interconnection Agreement (ZGIA), is currently pending action at the Commission in Docket No. 
ER26-3552.  
 
The issuance of the Commission’s Show Cause Order has reinforced the value of MISO’s 
prior efforts with stakeholders through the stakeholder process, including most recently the Large 
Load Working Group, to develop critical solutions to help support the cost-effective, reliable and 
efficient integration of Large Loads.  MISO continues working diligently with stakeholders on 
several additional initiatives in response to the Show Cause Order and is committed to bringing 
those solutions to the Commission in a timely manner.  
 
MISO appreciates the critical need to reliably integrate Large Loads.  Recent whitepapers 
and alerts published by the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) Large 
Loads Task Force and Large Loads Working Group identify emerging Large Loads as an increasing 
reliability consideration for the Bulk Electric System.  NERC guidance highlights that traditional 
planning and operational assumptions developed for conventional load may not fully capture the

change demand rapidly, and rely more heavily on power-electronic equipment.  
 
While NERC processes are underway to develop industry wide guidelines, the MISO 
region cannot wait to put in place needed interconnection reliability requirements to reliably 
integrate these near-term Large Loads.  Developing standards within the MISO region in advance 
of the NERC Standards process is not new.  MISO has similarly acted in the past to establish 
requirements for the interconnection of inverter-based resources in advance of the development of 
NERC Standards relating to such resources.  As Large Load growth accelerates across the MISO 
region these additional reliability considerations and processes are necessary to support 
transmission planning, operational preparedness, disturbance performance, and system stability, 
particularly given the unique characteristics of these facilities.  
 
To support the integration of these new large loads into the MISO system, the IRR Proposal 
establishes a reliability-based framework for Large Loads that complements existing MISO 
planning, interconnection, and operational processes.  The framework is designed to improve 
visibility into Large Load characteristics and behavior, support reliable planning and operational 
decision-making, and establish scalable and technically justified expectations proportional to 
demonstrated reliability risk.  The proposed framework focuses on four categories of reliability 
requirements that will be applicable to Large Loads.  The proposed reliability requirements will 
apply to MISO Transmission Customers providing Transmission Service the Large Load since the 
Transmission Customer is the entity that has a direct relationship with MISO.  The four categories 
of reliability requirements are as follows:  
 
1. 
Visibility Requirements – Data, Modeling, Telemetry, and Forecasting 
Requirements: These requirements establish expectations for facility information, 
electrical models, real-time telemetry, monitoring, short-term and forecasting, and 
other operational visibility requirements necessary to support planning studies, 
operational assessments, and accurate representation of Large Loads behavior and 
system impacts.   
2  
Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) Requirements: In addition to the broader 
visibility requirements above, the PMU requirements establish enhanced 
monitoring expectations for Computation Loads through high-resolution, time-
synchronized measurements.  PMU data provides MISO with greater visibility into 
facility behavior during system disturbances and rapid operating changes, 
supporting model validation, performance verification, disturbance analysis, and 
identification of potential dynamic interactions with the Transmission System. 
3. 
Ramp Requirements: These requirements 
address 
the rate at 
which 
Computational Loads may increase or decrease consumption during stable-state 
transitions.  Managing rapid changes in demand helps reduce real-time supply-
demand imbalances, sudden change in transmission power flows, and associated 
operational impacts, while supporting more reliable system operation.  Ramp-rate

limits do not apply during fault or disturbance conditions when necessary for 
equipment protection or to satisfy ride-through performance requirements. 
4. 
Ride-Through Requirements: These provisions establish minimum disturbance 
performance requirements applicable to Computational Load during voltage and 
frequency disturbances to reduce the risk of unnecessary disconnection or 
customer-initiated rapid reductions in Demands during credible system events.   
MISO recognizes that the Commission also included the need to develop a study process 
that addresses the unique operational and reliability challenges that providing transmission service 
to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads presents to the transmission system in its discussion 
of ongoing operational requirements in the Show Cause Order.6  MISO currently conducts such 
studies as part of its stability assessment in the MTEP and EPR processes. The IRR Proposal 
addresses requirements applicable to Large Load facilities themselves.  MISO intends to address 
enhancements to stability assessment study processes in a future Federal Power Act section 205 
filing.  Those future study processes will focus on identifying system-level reliability impacts 
associated with load additions and determining whether transmission or other system-level 
solutions are necessary, as part of a broader set of load addition and transmission service study 
requirements. 
   
MISO appreciates the guidance provided by the Commission through the Show Cause 
Orders as well as its allowance for regional flexibility to develop tailored solutions that meet the 
underlying regional needs and that can support the underlying regional processes.  The challenges 
and opportunities for large load integration differ across regions.  MISO’s expedited stakeholder 
process, in coordination with the MISO Transmission Owners and States, continues through the 
Large Load Working Group.   
 
The previously submitted ZGIA filing and the instant IRR Proposal are the initial steps in 
a broader set of solutions to address the concerns expressed by the Commission in the Show Cause 
Order and to meet the evolving needs of the MISO region.  In addition to the ZGIA and this IRR 
Proposal, MISO continues to develop a series of additional proposals that it plans to the 
Commission in advance of the November 16, 2026, deadline established based on the 
Commission’s abeyance of the Show Cause Order.  First, MISO is refining its Load Addition and 
Resource Study (“LARS”) process to facilitate the parallel study of load and generation that will 
address service to proximate load and support critical speed to power needs.  In addition, MISO is 
working to finalize its Firm Service Step Up proposal, which will provide a practical path to 
provide firm service increases over time as available.  In addition, MISO will work with its 
Transmission Owners and the States to develop and submit the additional proposals to: 1) provide 
additional transmission service products to facilitate Large Load integration; 2) enhance the Large 
Load application and study processes; and, 3) develop additional provisions to address potential 
cost-shifts associated with Large Load additions.

II. 
BACKGROUND 
A. 
Large Load Challenges  
 
The United States is in the midst of an unprecedented energy transition.  Large Load 
customers, including artificial intelligence (“AI”) data centers and next-generation manufacturing 
technologies, are driving a surge in interconnection requests. 7  As NERC has observed, the largest 
contributor to this accelerated demand growth is data center additions, with 18 GW of data center 
loads projected by 2035.8  The MISO region is no exception to this energy transition.  Energy-
intensive loads such as data centers, manufacturing expansion, and electrification are adding 
sustained, concentrated load at levels not seen in decades.9  While electricity demand growth has 
been relatively flat with an annual average of just 0.5% between 2009 and 2024, MISO is 
projecting a substantial increase of 1% to 2% per year through 2044, with even higher growth rates 
in the near term.10   
 
This growth has understandably drawn the focus of Relevant Electric Retail Rate 
Authorities (“RERRA”), stakeholders and federal policymakers.  On January 23, 2025, President 
Trump issued an Executive Order stating, “[i]t is the policy of the United States to sustain and 
enhance America’s global AI dominance in order to promote human flourishing, economic 
competitiveness, and national security.”11  On July 23, 2025, an Executive Order titled 
“Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure,” the Trump Administration 
announced its intention to pursue bold, large-scale industrial plans to incentivize critical 
manufacturing and data center development:  
 
We will pursue bold, large-scale industrial plans to vault the United 
States further into the lead on critical manufacturing processes and 
technologies that are essential to national security, economic 
prosperity, and scientific leadership.  These plans include artificial 
intelligence (AI) data centers and infrastructure that powers them, 
including high-voltage transmission lines and other equipment.  It 
will be a priority of my Administration to facilitate the rapid and

On October 23, 2025, the Secretary of Energy directed the Commission to consider an 
Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”) focused on the timely and orderly 
interconnection of Large Loads to the interstate transmission system.13  The Secretary’s 
correspondence to the Commission in support of the ANOPR emphasized the importance of the 
timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory integration of Large Loads:   
 
To usher in a new era of American prosperity, we must ensure all 
Americans and domestic industries have access to affordable, 
reliable, and secure electricity.  To do this, Large Loads, including 
AI data centers, served by public utilities must be able to connect to 
the transmission system in a timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory 
manner.  This is an urgent issue that requires prompt attention.14 
 
On June 18, 2026, the Commission issued the Show Cause Order.15  The Show Cause Order 
recognizes the unprecedented increase in requests for transmission service to serve Large Loads 
along with the growing interest in co-location arrangements to serve those Large Loads.16  As 
relevant to this filing, the Show Cause Order finds that MISO’s Tariff appears to be unjust and 
unreasonable because it lacks provisions addressing ongoing operational requirements for 
transmission customers taking transmission service on behalf of Large Loads.17  The Show Cause 
Order raises concerns that MISO’s Tariff does not require transmission customers to provide MISO 
hourly forecasts, telemetry data, and other data to ensure sufficient visibility or specify 
requirements for maintaining communication channels between MISO and the transmission 
customer on behalf of the Large Load.18  In addition, the Show Cause Order raises concerns that 
MISO’s Tariff does not specify ramp rate or ride-through requirements with which the transmission 
customer taking transmission service on behalf of the Large Load must comply.19  This filing 
proposes Tariff revisions establishing necessary ongoing operational requirements for Large Loads 
in response to the concerns stated in the Show Cause Order.

B. 
Addressing the Influx of Large Loads in the MISO Region 
 
As noted above, the MISO region is experiencing a significant increase in both the scale 
and pace of Large Load development.  As indicated in the chart below, MISO’s 2026 Long-Term 
Load Forecast indicates that the region is experiencing load growth at levels not seen in decades, 
driven in large part by unprecedented large load activity and accelerating project announcements.20  
Data centers and advanced manufacturing are among the primary drivers of this growth, with some 
projects seeking to develop on timelines significantly shorter than those traditionally associated 
with generation and transmission infrastructure.  This combination of increased volume and 
accelerated development is changing the manner in which MISO must plan for and reliably 
integrate new load. 
 
 
 
Recent whitepapers and alerts published by the NERC Large Loads Task Force and Large 
Loads Working Group identify emerging Large Loads as an increasing reliability consideration for 
the Bulk Electric System.21  NERC guidance highlights that traditional planning and operational 
assumptions developed for conventional load may not fully capture the behavior or reliability 
impacts of emerging large loads, particularly as load facilities become larger, capable of rapid 
demand changes , and increasingly interconnected with power-electronic equipment.

Accommodating accelerated interconnection of Large Loads requires MISO to ensure that 
it can reliably plan for and operate the Transmission System as these facilities come online.  Key 
reliability considerations include sufficient visibility into Large Load characteristics and operating 
behavior, accurate forecasting and modeling, and requirements that address operational risks, such 
as rapid change in Demand, disturbance response, including ride-through capability.    
 
MISO, its member States, and a broad and diverse group of stakeholders have been 
developing multiple initiatives to address evolving system conditions and to support efficient and 
reliable interconnection of Large Loads prior to and after the issuance of the Show Cause Order.  
For example, MISO recently implemented the Expedited Resource Addition Study (“ERAS”) as a 
targeted, temporary process to issue a Generator Interconnection Agreement in three months.  
MISO also improved its Transmission Expansion Plan’s EPR process to quickly approve 
transmission upgrades necessary to address urgent needs associated with the addition of Large 
Loads.  Further, MISO initiated the MISO-SPP Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue Study 
(“JTIQ”), which aims at building transmission network upgrades along the MISO-SPP seams to 
enable large amounts of new generation to come online in a more timely manner.   
     
While these initiatives provide important benefits, they do not fully address the reliability 
and operational challenges associated with accelerating Large Load growth.  Existing planning 
reforms primarily focus on generation additions and transmission development timelines.  
Likewise, broader reliability initiatives were not specifically designed to address the unique 
characteristics and operational challenges presented by Large Load and Computational Load 
additions.  As the size and concentration of these facilities increase, additional visibility into load 
behavior and system interactions is necessary to support reliable operation of the Transmission 
System.  
 
Accordingly, MISO recognizes that additional Tariff-based solutions are necessary to 
establish clear reliability expectations, improve operational visibility, and facilitate timely 
integration of Large Loads in a manner that is both reliable and non-discriminatory.  These 
solutions must also consider and address the unique planning and operational characteristics of 
Large Load interconnection customers and hyperscale data centers, in particular.    
 
MISO is moving quickly and engaging with stakeholders through the Large Load Working 
Group (“LLWG”), as well as with the Organization of MISO States, Inc. (“OMS”), in an expedited 
manner to develop the broader set of solutions outlined in the August 3, 2026, motion filed by 
MISO and the MISO Transmission Owners to hold all proceedings related to the Show Cause 
Order in abeyance for 90 days.22  The Abeyance Motion explained that MISO and the MISO 
Transmission Owners required additional time to continue the stakeholder process and submit FPA

III. 
OVERVIEW OF THE IRR PROPOSAL AND HOW IT ADDRESSES THE SHOW CAUSE ORDER 
The IRR Proposal establishes broad categories of reliability requirements intended to 
address planning, operational and disturbance performance associated with Large Loads, along 
with new definitions, applicability and transition provisions necessary to implement the new 
requirements.  A brief overview of each component of the filing is summarized below: 
 
• 
Definitions and Applicability: Establishes which facilities qualify as Large Loads and 
Computational Loads and identifies when the requirements apply. 
 
• 
Data Requirements: Establishes the facility and operational information MISO needs 
to understand Large Load characteristics and expected behavior. 
 
• 
Model Requirements: Requires appropriate electrical models so Large Loads can be 
accurately represented in MISO planning and operational analyses. 
 
• 
Telemetry Requirements: Provides real-time visibility into Large Load demand and 
operating conditions to support reliable system operations. 
 
• 
Forecasting Requirements: Establishes short-term and other forecast information 
needed to anticipate Large Load demand and operating changes. 
 
• 
PMU Requirements for Computational Loads: Provides high-resolution, time-
synchronized measurements to support disturbance analysis, model validation, and 
performance verification.

MISO further notes that this filing incorporates a proposed Tariff definition of “Large 
Load.”  This proposed definition is intended to apply to this filing as well as the other filings in 
response to the Show Cause Order, as applicable.  
A. 
New Definitions Related to the IRR for Large Load 
 
 
1. 
Large Load 
The Order posits that MISO’s Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks 
a definition of Large Load sufficient to capture loads that present the unique challenges associated 
with Large Loads.28  This filing proposes to address the Order’s concern by implementing a clear 
and consistent Large Load definition, as follows:   
Large Load:  Load with Demand of 50 MW or more associated with 
any facility or aggregation of facilities located at a single substation 
behind one or more Point(s) of Withdrawal from the Transmission 
System that is owned, operated, or controlled by: (a) a single entity 
or (b) a group of entities that will coordinate with respect to the 
profile of the Load.  Large Load does not include Load used 
exclusively for charging an Electric Storage Resource. 
 
As explained by Ms. Li, MISO developed the proposed Large Load definition through a 
review of emerging industry practices, consideration of the reliability needs in the MISO region, 
and stakeholder feedback.29  Based on that review, MISO selected a 50 MW threshold as a 
reasonable and administratively clear starting point, consistent with industry precedent and 
sufficiently significant to warrant application of MISO’s Large Load requirements.  The definition 
is based on gross load rather than net load so that MISO has visibility into the full electrical demand 
and characteristics of the facility.  Further, MISO defined Large Load at the facility or site level to 
allow loads under common ownership or coordinated operational control at a single site to be 
considered together, including where the site is served through multiple points of interconnection.

Load.30 
 
2. 
Computational Load 
This filing also proposes a new definition of Computational Load in order to further support 
the consistent interpretation of the proposed reliability framework described in this filing, as 
follows: 
Computational Load: Large Load comprised of 25 MW or more of 
Demand from information technology equipment, such as servers, 
storage, and networking hardware. 
As explained by Ms. Li, the Computational Load definition distinguishes a subset of Large Loads 
that may exhibit operational characteristics different from more traditional loads, including rapid 
changes in demand, highly coordinated control behavior, and power-electronic responses during 
system disturbances.31  This distinction allows MISO to apply certain incremental requirements—
such as Ramp, PMU, and Ride-Through requirements—only where those characteristics warrant 
additional reliability consideration.  The Computational Load definition is necessary as certain 
proposed requirements are intended to apply only to Large Loads with operating characteristics 
that warrant additional reliability consideration.  Computational Loads may exhibit rapid and 
coordinated changes in demand, significant power-electronic behavior, and distinct responses to 
Transmission System disturbances.  Defining Computational Load supports a more targeted and 
risk-informed approach, rather than applying the same requirements to all Large Loads regardless 
of facility type or operating behavior.   
B. 
Applicability of the Interconnection Reliability Requirements 
 
The requirements in this filing will apply to Large Loads as established in the MISO Tariff 
and the Business Practices Manual for Large Load.  Subject to the transition provisions discussed 
below, all Large Loads will be subject to the applicable visibility requirements including: Basic 
Facility Data, Modeling, Telemetry, Forecast Data, and Audit requirements.  In addition, the 
Computational Load component of a Large Load, as defined in the Tariff, is subject to the PMU, 
Ride-Through, and Ramp requirements.  MISO recognizes that not all Large Loads present the 
same reliability risks and has limited the application of PMU, Ramp, and Ride-Through 
requirements to the Computational Load component of a Large Load, which reflects the increased 
operational risk Computational Loads place on the Transmission System.  Ms. Li explains that the 
IRR Proposal is intended to provide a scalable and risk-informed framework that may be applied

The Transmission Customer taking Transmission Service on behalf of a Large Load will 
be responsible for ensuring compliance by the Large Load with each of the applicable requirements 
set forth in the new Tariff section 37A.33  Requiring the Transmission Customer to ensure 
compliance with the requirements established in the IRR Proposal is consistent with the Show 
Cause Order’s discussion of imposing requirements on an “Eligible Customer” and recognizes that 
the ultimate owner of a Large Load may not participate directly in MISO’s markets or otherwise 
have contractual privity to MISO.  All Large Loads interconnected to the Transmission System, 
however, will be required to procure Transmission Service, through a Transmission Customer, 
pursuant to the Tariff.  As such, the Transmission Customer will be required to enter into a 
Transmission Service agreement, which incorporates by reference the terms of the Tariff, including 
the requirements proposed herein.  As a result, applying the requirements established in the IRR 
Proposal to a Transmission Customer taking Transmission Service on behalf of a Large Load 
establishes a legally enforceable framework though which all reliability requirements imposed on 
a Large Load may be enforced. 
The Show Cause Order indicates that MISO’s Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable 
because it lacks  pro forma provisions in a transmission service agreement between MISO and the 
transmission customer taking transmission service on behalf of a large load to memorialize the 
ongoing operational requirements similar to those proposed herein.34  The Commission notes that, 
without such  pro forma provisions in a transmission service agreement between MISO and the 
transmission customer, MISO may be unable to enforce ongoing operational requirements for 
transmission customers taking transmission service on behalf of large loads, and states that MISO 
should explain whether the Tariff remains just and reasonable without such pro forma provisions 
in a transmission service agreement, or propose revisions to include pro forma provisions 
memorializing the ongoing operational requirements in a transmission service agreement between 
MISO and the transmission customer.35

General Principles  
Ride-through requirements apply at the facility’s Point(s) of Withdrawal (PoW(s)) and 
establish the voltage and frequency conditions under which a Computational Loads are required 
to remain connected to the Transmission System and continue operation during disturbances. 
When system conditions remain within the specified ride-through performance limits,

unnecessary interruption of service.  As Ms. Li notes, protection and control systems should be 
coordinated to avoid unnecessary tripping, and momentary cessation is not permitted unless 
explicitly allowed.  Following disturbance clearance, Computational Loads are expected to recover 
toward pre-disturbance operating conditions in a controlled manner consistent with established 
performance expectations.50

MISO proposes this Subsection 37A.4 to ensure that Transmission Customers provide

subsection strikes the appropriate balance of providing all parties with sufficient detail regarding 
the proposed forecast data requirements while leaving implementation details to the Business 
Practices Manual.

proposing a new subsection detailing the PMU requirements for Large Loads.  
The proposed subsection states that Computational Load is subject to the PMU 
requirements.  The subsection requires PMU and recording information to be 
installed before the Service Commencement Date of a Large Load or September 
1, 2027 (whichever is later), and requires that this equipment gather the 
requirements specified in the Business Practices Manual.  The proposed 
subsections allow for the use of existing equipment to meet these requirements, 
provided that equipment can collect data at the same rate as PMU and which 
data is synchronized via a high-accuracy satellite clock.  The proposed 
subsection specifies that the PMU equipment must be installed at the 
Transmission Owner’s side of the Point(s) of Withdrawal and become part of 
the Transmission Owner interconnection facilities.   
MISO proposes this Subsection 37A.5 to implement PMU requirements for Large Loads.  
The subjection ensures that those PMU requirements are satisfied by either the installation new 
equipment or a demonstration that existing equipment can serve substantially the same purpose.  
The subsection thus strikes a reasonable balance of requiring the installation of new equipment 
with grandfathering existing equipment that serves substantially the same purpose.  The proposed 
subsection also strikes the appropriate balance of providing all parties with sufficient detail of the 
PMU requirements while leaving implementation details to the Business Practices Manual.

V. 
STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT 
MISO has engaged in detailed discussions with stakeholders on Large Load issues since 
2024 in various stakeholder entities and workshops.  MISO first discussed Large Loads with 
stakeholders in the context of Expedited Project Review process improvements at the Planning 
Advisory Committee (“PAC”) and Planning Subcommittee (“PSC”) in 2024 and 2025.  Moreover, 
since 2024, MISO has discussed coordinating the MISO Transmission Expansion Plan and 
Definitive Planning Phases (“DPP”) processes to accommodate Large Loads at the PSC.  MISO 
additionally discussed Large Load citing methodology at the November 18, 2025, Futures 
Redesign Workshop. 
 
 
MISO introduced the Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements at the Large 
Loads Workshop on January 30, 2026.52  The workshop addressed the challenges associated with 
reliably interconnecting Large Loads, focusing on defining reliability requirements and improving 
the speed of integration while maintaining reliability to support member plans and goals.  
Following the January 30th workshop, MISO discussed the Large Load Interconnection Reliability 
Requirements at the PAC and the Large Load Working Group (“LLWG”).  A table of meetings 
involving MISO’s Large Load reliability requirements development, with links to meeting 
materials is provided as an attachment to Ms. Li’s testimony. 
 
 
At the February 25, 2026, PAC, MISO proposed a definition of Large Load and provided 
a high-level overview of the Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements.  MISO 
requested stakeholder feedback on the Large Load definition.  At the April 20, 2026, LLWG, MISO 
provided a revised Large Load definition based on stakeholder feedback and presented the Large 
Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements.  MISO requested feedback on the Large Load 
Interconnection Reliability Requirements.  At the April 22, 2026, PAC, MISO shared the revised 
Large Load definition that had been shared previously at the LLWG.  MISO additionally presented 
transition provisions it developed to address pending but unbuilt Large Load.  
 
 
At the May 14, 2026, LLWG, MISO responded to stakeholder feedback from the April 20 
LLWG meeting, provided proposed Tariff language for the Large Load Interconnection Reliability 
Requirements, and provided an updated Large Load definition.  In response to stakeholder 
feedback MISO revised the applicability language to provide additional clarity, included 
transitional provisions that offer flexibility during implementation, and incorporated a phased-in 
implementation to support readiness across customers and utilities.  MISO additionally updated its

around applicability, transition provisions, and requirement specific language.  Namely, MISO: (1) 
updated Tariff and BPM language to clarify treatment of existing loads, any expansions, and the 
applicability date; (2) updated the transitional provision to allow more flexibility; (3) updated the 
Applicability section to distinguish between Computational and Non-Computational Loads, and 
applied only ramp, PMU, ride-through, and advanced modeling requirements to Computational 
Loads; (4) updated the Large Load Customer definition to clearly define roles and responsibilities; 
(5) expanded process detail across several Tariff sections, including applicability screening, pre-
MTEP/EPR timing, and transitional provisions for inflight projects; and (6) clarified that Tariff 
applicability for the ramp, PMU, and ride-through requirements align with NERC’s emerging 
definition of Computational Loads and NERC’s Load Modeling Task Force technical discussions.  
MISO additionally revised the Large Load definition by removing the Large Load Campus 
construct in response to stakeholder feedback.  In addition, MISO published a technical 
compendium outlining the technical details of the proposal that will establish the basis of the 
Business Practice Manual (“BPM”) for Large Load. 
 
 
At the June 29, 2026, LLWG, MISO reviewed Tariff redlines for the Large Load definition 
and Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements based on stakeholder feedback.

applicability, transition provisions, and requirement specific language.  MISO additionally 
described how its proposed framework is consistent with the Commission’s Show Cause Order 
and noted that the framework is also in line with the emerging NERC guidance and broader 
industry practices.  Furthermore, MISO described how its interconnection framework relies on the 
Tariff to set requirements and its BPM to guide consistent implementation, noting that it is 
targeting Large Load BPM development to take place from June to September 2026.  MISO 
requested stakeholder feedback on the Tariff updates.  
 
MISO separately presented on Large Load Telemetry and PMU Requirements, with the 
purpose of establishing SCADA telemetry requirements for Large Loads, and PMU requirements 
for Computational Loads to provide situational awareness and support system reliability across the 
MISO footprint.  Specifically, MISO will require real-time SCADA telemetry from Large Loads 
via ICCP to support real-time monitoring and analysis, and real-time SCADA telemetry from 
generation behind same POI as Large Load will also be required for real-time monitoring and 
optimal market dispatch; generator telemetry shall not be netted with load.  Furthermore, MISO
